title: Offer and invitation to treat
subtitle: Where a genuine offer begins — and where it doesn't
objectives: Distinguish a legally operative offer from a mere invitation to treat across shop displays, advertisements, and negotiations
Explain how a unilateral offer differs from an ordinary bilateral offer, and why it can be accepted by performance alone
Identify the four ways an offer can be terminated and apply them correctly to a new fact pattern

leadingAuthorities.citation: Carlill v Carbolic Smoke Ball Co [1893] 1 QB 256
leadingAuthorities.role: A unilateral offer made to the whole world, accepted by performing the stipulated act

leadingAuthorities.citation: Pharmaceutical Society of Great Britain v Boots Cash Chemists [1953] 1 QB 401
leadingAuthorities.role: A self-service shop shelf is an invitation to treat; the customer makes the offer at the till
Displaying goods in a shop window is an invitation to treat, not an offer for sale
A newspaper advertisement is ordinarily an invitation to treat, given limited stock

leadingAuthorities.citation: Gibson v Manchester City Council [1979] 1 WLR 294
leadingAuthorities.role: Whether a communication is an offer turns on its actual language and context, not any special rule

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Most students can define 'offer' in the abstract but lose marks the moment a shop window or an advert appears in the facts. Where the profile shows application lagging behind knowledge, this brief note appears: 'You know the definition — this lesson is about the traps built around it.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've scored well on the bare definitions here before. The test pool below leans hard on application: expect fact patterns dressed up as shops, adverts and auctions, not textbook questions.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 1 and don't rush the objective test for what counts as an offer — every later part in this lesson assumes you can state it cold.

overview.hook: A flick-knife sits in a shop window with a price tag. A newspaper advert offers wild birds for sale. A smoke ball promises £100 to anyone who catches flu after using it as directed, with £1,000 sitting in a bank account to prove the company means it. Only one of these three is a legally binding offer — and knowing which, and why, is the single most commonly mis-answered distinction in the whole of contract law.
overview.lawStatedNotice: Law stated as at 22 September 2026. The offer/invitation to treat distinction is long-settled common law; no legislative change is pending.

parts.heading: Offer, invitation, and the difference exams live on
body: A contract needs an offer and an acceptance that mirrors it. That sounds simple until you try to say, precisely, what an offer actually is. The working definition: a clear statement of terms, made with the objective intention to be bound the instant the other side agrees, and communicated to the person meant to accept it.

An invitation to treat looks similar on the surface — it can use the same words, appear in the same places, even quote a price — but it is legally a different act entirely. It invites the other party to make an offer; it does not commit the person making it to anything. The seller who displays a price is usually saying 'come and make me an offer at this price', not 'I am bound to sell to the first person who agrees.'

The test the courts apply is objective, not subjective: would a reasonable person, reading the words and context, conclude that the maker intended to be bound without further negotiation? Motive and hope don't matter. Language, context, and commercial common sense do. That objective test is the thread running through every case in this lesson — memorise the individual cases, but understand that they are all applications of the same single question.

components.definition: A communication inviting others to make offers — it is not itself capable of acceptance and creates no binding commitment, however definite it may look on its face.

interaction.prompt: A television is displayed in a shop window with a price tag of £199. On the general rule alone, is this display a legally binding offer to sell at that price?
options: No — a price-tagged display is ordinarily only an invitation to treat
Yes — a price tag is a binding offer to any customer who wants it
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Correct. A displayed price invites customers to make an offer to buy — it doesn't commit the shop to sell, no matter how clear the tag looks.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Not quite — a price tag in a window is the textbook example of an invitation to treat, not an offer. Keep that distinction in mind as the cases in this lesson unpack why it matters.

parts.heading: The shop shelf and the locked window: Boots and Fisher v Bell
body: Picture a self-service chemist. Medicines sit on open shelves; a customer picks one up, walks to the till, and a pharmacist supervises the sale. If the shelf display were itself an offer, the contract would form the moment the customer's hand touched the bottle — before the pharmacist had any chance to intervene on a controlled substance. That was the practical problem the Pharmaceutical Society sued over.

The Court of Appeal held that the shelf display is only an invitation to treat. The customer makes the offer by bringing the item to the till; the shop accepts (or refuses) it at that point, with the pharmacist able to step in beforehand. This isn't a technicality — it's the rule that lets a shop refuse a sale to someone underage, or correct a mispriced item, right up until the till accepts. If you're advising a retailer nervous about being 'forced' to sell at a mistaken price, this is the case that reassures them.

Fisher v Bell applies exactly the same logic to a criminal statute. A shopkeeper displayed a flick-knife in his window with a price ticket, and was prosecuted under legislation making it an offence to 'offer for sale' such a weapon. The court held that, in ordinary contract law terms, a window display is an invitation to treat, not an offer for sale — so no offence under that particular wording had been committed. Parliament later closed the loophole by amending the statute, but the contract-law reasoning behind the case remains the standard authority for shop window displays generally.

components.caseName: Pharmaceutical Society of Great Britain v Boots Cash Chemists (Southern) Ltd
components.factsShort: In a self-service pharmacy, a customer selected medicine from an open shelf and paid at a till supervised by a pharmacist. The Pharmaceutical Society argued the sale occurred, unsupervised, when the item was taken from the shelf.
components.ratioShort: The shelf display is an invitation to treat; the customer offers to buy at the till, and the shop accepts (or refuses) there, with supervision intact.

expanded.facts: Boots operated a 'self-service' layout in which customers picked items — including some medicines listed under the Pharmacy and Poisons Act 1933 as requiring sale under pharmacist supervision — from open shelves before paying at a cash till where a registered pharmacist was stationed. The Pharmaceutical Society argued this arrangement was unlawful because the 'sale' occurred at the shelf, unsupervised.
expanded.judgmentExtract: The Court of Appeal held that displaying goods on a shelf, even with a price attached, is an invitation to the customer to make an offer to buy; the customer does so by presenting the item at the till, and the contract is completed only when the cashier (with the pharmacist supervising) accepts that offer. Until that moment, the customer remains free to put the item back, and the shop remains free to decline the sale.
expanded.significance: This is the anchor authority for treating any self-service or shelf-based display as an invitation to treat rather than an offer. It matters commercially because it preserves the seller's freedom to refuse a sale — for age-restricted goods, mispriced items, or limited stock — right up until the moment of payment.

components.factsShort: A shopkeeper displayed a flick-knife in his window with a price ticket and was prosecuted for 'offering for sale' an offensive weapon.
components.ratioShort: A window display with a price is an invitation to treat, not an offer for sale, applying ordinary contract-law meaning to the statutory phrase.

expanded.facts: The defendant, a shopkeeper, placed a flick-knife in his shop window next to a ticket showing its price. He was charged under the Restriction of Offensive Weapons Act 1959 with offering the knife for sale, an offence under that Act.
expanded.judgmentExtract: The court applied the established contract-law meaning of 'offer' and held that a window display, however precisely priced, is in law only an invitation to treat — an invitation for a customer to come in and make an offer to buy. Because the statute used the specific words 'offer for sale', and the display was not in law an offer, the defendant had not committed the statutory offence as drafted.
expanded.significance: Fisher v Bell shows the offer/invitation to treat distinction operating outside pure contract disputes, in the interpretation of a criminal statute — and is often cited as an example of the literal rule of statutory interpretation. Parliament subsequently amended the legislation to cover displays as well as offers, but the underlying contract-law point about window displays remains good law.

interaction.prompt: Tap the fact in this scenario that marks the moment the offer is actually made.
interaction.scenarioText: In a self-service supermarket, Priya takes a bottle of wine from an open shelf, carries it around the store for ten minutes, and then places it on the checkout belt in front of the cashier.
tappableSpans: takes a bottle of wine from an open shelf
carries it around the store for ten minutes
places it on the checkout belt in front of the cashier
interaction.correctSpan: places it on the checkout belt in front of the cashier
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. Following Boots, the shelf is only an invitation to treat — Priya makes the offer to buy at the till, and the cashier's acceptance completes the contract there.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look again at where the offer sits under Boots — it isn't the moment Priya picks the item up, however long she then carries it around. The offer is made when she presents it for payment.

parts.heading: Advertisements: usually an invitation, except when the world is invited to accept
body: In 1893, a London company sold a device called the Carbolic Smoke Ball, and placed newspaper advertisements promising £100 to any user who caught influenza after using it as directed, three times daily, for two weeks. To show they were serious, the company said it had deposited £1,000 at a bank 'shewing our sincerity in the matter'. Mrs Louisa Carlill used the smoke ball exactly as instructed, caught flu anyway, and sued for her £100.

The company argued the advert was mere advertising puff, or at most an invitation to treat — you can't make a binding offer to the entire world, they said, because there'd be no way to know who had 'accepted'. The Court of Appeal disagreed on every point. The advert was specific and promissory, not vague puffery; the £1,000 deposit showed a genuine intention to be bound; and while an offer to the whole world is unusual, it is perfectly binding as to whichever member of the public actually performs the stipulated act.

This is a unilateral offer: a promise made in exchange for an act, rather than in exchange for a matching promise. Crucially, the offeree accepts by performing — Mrs Carlill didn't need to write back and say 'I accept', because using the smoke ball as directed was itself both the acceptance and full performance at once. Compare this to Partridge v Crittenden, where a newspaper advertisement offered wild birds for sale: the court held that was an ordinary invitation to treat, because the advertiser had a limited stock and could not sensibly be taken to promise a sale to every single reader who replied. The difference is not 'advert versus no advert' — it's whether the words and circumstances show a genuine, unlimited promise to be bound (Carlill) or an invitation constrained by scarce supply (Partridge).

components.caseName: Carlill v Carbolic Smoke Ball Co
components.factsShort: A company advertised a £100 reward to anyone who used its smoke ball as directed and still caught influenza, backing the promise with a £1,000 bank deposit.
components.ratioShort: An advertisement can be a genuine unilateral offer to the whole world where its terms are specific and promissory; it is accepted by performing the stipulated act, without any need to communicate acceptance in advance.

expanded.facts: The Carbolic Smoke Ball Company advertised that its product would prevent influenza, and promised £100 to any purchaser who used it as directed and nonetheless caught the illness, stating a £1,000 deposit had been made at a bank to demonstrate sincerity. Mrs Carlill bought and used the smoke ball as instructed, caught influenza, and claimed the £100. The company refused to pay, arguing the advert was not a serious offer.
expanded.judgmentExtract: The Court of Appeal held that the advertisement's language was too definite to be mere puff, that the deposit was strong evidence of a genuine intention to be bound, and that an offer can validly be made to the whole world, to be accepted by whichever member of the public performs the specified conditions. Communication of acceptance in advance was not required, because the very nature of the offer — a promise in return for an act — waived that requirement; performance of the act was itself both acceptance and consideration.
expanded.significance: Carlill remains the leading authority for unilateral contracts and for offers made to an unascertained group. It establishes that performance of the stipulated act can constitute acceptance without prior notice to the offeror, and that a sufficiently definite advertisement, especially one backed by evidence of serious intent, can be a true offer rather than an invitation to treat.

components.definition: An offer made in exchange for the performance of an act (rather than a matching promise), which the offeree accepts simply by performing that act — no advance communication of acceptance is generally required.

interaction.prompt: What best explains why the Carbolic Smoke Ball advertisement was held to be an offer, while the wild-bird advertisement in Partridge v Crittenden was held to be only an invitation to treat?
options: Adverts in newspapers can never be offers, so Carlill must have been decided on some other document

The Carlill advert's specific, promissory language and the bank deposit showed genuine intent to be bound to anyone who performed; the Partridge advert was constrained by limited stock, so could not sensibly bind the seller to every reader
Carlill involved a company and Partridge involved an individual, and only companies can make offers to the world
interaction.trapExplanation: The tempting wrong answers try to draw a bright line by document type ('adverts are never offers') or by the identity of the advertiser — neither is the actual test. What matters, in both cases, is the same objective question: do the words and circumstances show a genuine, unconstrained promise to be bound?

parts.heading: Gibson v Manchester City Council: when words alone decide the outcome
body: Consider two readings of the same kind of letter. Mr Gibson wrote to his local council asking about buying his council house. The council's Treasurer replied that the council 'may be prepared to sell' the house to him at a stated price, and added: 'This letter should not be regarded as a firm offer.' Gibson filled in and returned the enclosed application form. Before contracts were exchanged, political control of the council changed, and the new council refused to proceed.

Reading one: this is all just cautious council paperwork, and courts shouldn't let a change of heart escape liability on a technicality of wording. Reading two: the council's language was doing real, deliberate work — 'may be prepared' and 'not a firm offer' are about as clear a signal as a document can give that no offer is yet on the table.

The House of Lords firmly preferred reading two, and for a reason worth sitting with: Lord Diplock warned against inventing any special test for local authority correspondence, or indeed for any category of case. The exercise is always the same ordinary one — read the actual words used, in their actual context, and ask what a reasonable recipient would understand them to mean. Here, that exercise pointed only one way: an invitation to treat, inviting Gibson to make a formal application, which the council could still accept or reject.

The comparison that sharpens this is Storer v Manchester City Council, decided just before Gibson, where a council letter said 'I understand you will sign the Agreement and return it... if the Corporation agrees to this we will send you the Agreement for signature' — and the Court of Appeal read that as a genuine offer awaiting only Storer's signature. Same council, similar housing scheme, opposite outcome — because the words were different. That contrast is the whole lesson of Gibson: there is no shortcut past reading the document.

components.label: Reading correspondence for offer or invitation
points: No special rule exists for any category of correspondence — the same objective, contextual test applies to every case (Lord Diplock in Gibson)
Explicit disclaiming language ('may be prepared to sell', 'not a firm offer') is strong evidence of an invitation to treat, not an offer
Language committing to a defined next step ('we will send you the Agreement for signature', as in Storer) can tip a similar letter into being a genuine offer
Filling in and returning an application form is not itself acceptance if no offer existed yet to accept — it may just be the applicant's own offer

components.definition: Whether a communication is an offer is judged by how a reasonable person in the recipient's position would understand it, not by what the sender privately intended or hoped.

interaction.prompt: How confident are you that a letter stating 'we may be prepared to sell at this price... this letter should not be regarded as a firm offer' is, in law, an offer capable of acceptance?
interaction.explanation: Gibson settled this on very similar wording: explicit disclaiming language of this kind is treated as strong evidence that no offer is yet on the table, however far negotiations have progressed.

parts.heading: How an offer dies: revocation, lapse, rejection, counter-offer
body: An offer is not a permanent fixture waiting to be accepted whenever the offeree gets around to it. Four routes bring an offer to an end, and an exam fact pattern will usually be testing exactly one of them — spotting which is half the battle.

Revocation: the offeror withdraws the offer. This must actually be communicated to the offeree before acceptance — a change of mind kept private, or announced only after the other side has already accepted, comes too late. For a unilateral offer made to the world (the Carlill type), revocation generally has to be communicated with at least the same prominence as the original offer, and cannot defeat someone who has already substantially started performing in reliance on it.

Lapse of time: an offer that specifies a deadline dies automatically at that deadline; an offer with no stated deadline lapses after a 'reasonable time', which depends on the subject matter — an offer to sell a perishable or fast-moving item lapses far sooner than an offer over stable, unhurried terms.
Rejection: once the offeree says no, the offer is gone — the offeree cannot later change their mind and purport to accept the same offer, however soon afterwards.

Counter-offer: this is the one students most often miss, because it looks like a step towards agreement rather than the death of the original offer. Proposing different terms in response to an offer is treated as a rejection of that offer plus a new offer of the counter-offeror's own — the original offer cannot simply be revived by trying to accept it afterwards, unless the original offeror chooses to put it back on the table. The next lesson in this pathway builds an entire doctrine — the mirror image rule and the 'battle of the forms' — out of exactly this single idea.

components.label: The four ways an offer ends
points: Revocation — the offeror withdraws it, communicated before acceptance
Lapse of time — a stated deadline passes, or a 'reasonable time' expires with none stated
Rejection — the offeree says no, and cannot revive the offer by later purporting to accept it
Counter-offer — proposing different terms operates as a rejection of the original offer, not merely a negotiating step

components.title: An offer that dies by counter-offer

events.label: Seller offers house for £250,000
events.description: A valid, communicated offer on stated terms.

events.label: Buyer replies offering £240,000
events.description: This is a counter-offer — it rejects the £250,000 offer outright.

events.label: Seller does not respond
events.description: The original £250,000 offer no longer exists; it was killed at the counter-offer stage.

events.label: Buyer tries to 'accept' the original £250,000 offer
events.description: There is nothing left to accept — the buyer's own counter-offer is now the only offer on the table, awaiting the seller's response.

interaction.prompt: Put these events in the order needed to correctly identify when the original offer stopped existing.
items: A gallery offers a painting to a collector for £8,000
The gallery says nothing further for a week
The collector then tries to accept the original £8,000 offer
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Correct sequence. The offer effectively ends at step 2 — the counter-offer of £7,000 is a rejection of the £8,000 offer, so by step 4 there is nothing left for the collector to accept.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Check the order against when the offer actually dies. It ends the moment the collector counter-offers at £7,000 — everything after that is the collector trying to accept an offer that no longer exists.

testPool.prompt: State the objective test courts use to decide whether a communication is an offer or an invitation to treat.
acceptableAnswers: whether a reasonable person would understand it as showing intention to be bound without further negotiation
objective intention to be bound test
would a reasonable recipient think they could accept it and form a contract
testPool.modelAnswer: Whether a reasonable person, reading the words in their context, would conclude the maker intended to be bound the moment the other party agreed — judged objectively, not by the maker's private intention.

testPool.prompt: In Fisher v Bell, was displaying a flick-knife in a shop window with a price ticket held to be an 'offer for sale' under the relevant statute?
options: No — a window display is an invitation to treat, not an offer for sale
Yes — any priced display is automatically an offer for sale

testPool.prompt: Which of the following is NOT one of the four recognised ways an offer can be terminated?
options: Revocation
Lapse of time
The offeree telling a friend they intend to accept
Counter-offer
testPool.trapExplanation: Privately telling a third party you intend to accept has no legal effect on the offer at all — nothing happens to the offer unless the offeree actually communicates acceptance, rejection, or a counter-offer to the offeror.

testPool.prompt: The Restriction of Offensive Weapons Act 1959, as it stood in Fisher v Bell, made it an offence to 'offer for sale' certain weapons. Why did the ordinary contract-law meaning of 'offer' matter to a criminal prosecution?
options: Because the court applied the established contract-law meaning of 'offer', and a window display is not, in that sense, an offer, so the specific statutory wording was not satisfied
Because criminal statutes always incorporate whatever meaning is most favourable to the defendant, regardless of context
Because the contract-law meaning of 'offer' is irrelevant to criminal statutes and the court ignored it entirely

testPool.prompt: Order the reasoning steps a court follows in applying the Boots analysis to a self-service sale.
items: Classify the shelf display as an invitation to treat
Identify the moment the customer presents the item for payment as the offer
Ask whether the shop (via the till or supervising staff) accepts that offer
Confirm the contract completes only once acceptance occurs at the till

testPool.prompt: In the passage below adapted from Carlill v Carbolic Smoke Ball Co, highlight the sentence stating the ratio on communication of acceptance.
testPool.passage: The advertisement was not mere puffery, given its specific terms and the deposit evidencing sincerity. Where an offer is made in terms that show the offeror does not expect or require notice of acceptance before performance, the offeree accepts by performing the act requested, without needing to communicate that acceptance in advance. The company was accordingly bound to pay the promised sum.
testPool.ratioSentence: Where an offer is made in terms that show the offeror does not expect or require notice of acceptance before performance, the offeree accepts by performing the act requested, without needing to communicate that acceptance in advance.

testPool.prompt: Which scenario is closer to Carlill v Carbolic Smoke Ball Co than to Partridge v Crittenden?
testPool.scenarioA: A local newspaper advert says 'Vintage bicycles for sale, £150 each, limited stock available, call to arrange viewing.'
testPool.scenarioB: A national advert promises £500 to anyone who completes a specific marathon course within four hours wearing the sponsor's branded shoes, backed by a publicised prize fund.
testPool.explanation: B mirrors Carlill: a specific, promissory reward for performing a defined act, backed by evidence of serious intent, made to an unlimited group. A is closer to Partridge: a general advert constrained by limited stock, which cannot sensibly bind the seller to every single reader.

testPool.prompt: As a general starting position (before looking at specific wording), how confident should you be that a newspaper advertisement is a genuine offer rather than an invitation to treat?
sliderLabels: Very confident it's only an invitation to treat
testPool.explanation: Partridge v Crittenden sets the general starting presumption: adverts are usually invitations to treat because of limited stock. Carlill is the recognised exception where the wording and circumstances show a genuine, unconstrained promise.

testPool.prompt: A jeweller displays a ring in a locked glass cabinet with a card reading '£2,000'. A customer insists the jeweller must sell it to her at that price because it is 'clearly on offer'. Is the jeweller legally bound to sell?
options: No — the display, however precisely priced, is an invitation to treat under Fisher v Bell / Boots-style reasoning; the jeweller can decline
Yes — a price displayed on a specific, identifiable item is always a binding offer
Yes, but only because the item is in a locked cabinet rather than on an open shelf
testPool.explanation: The locked cabinet makes no legal difference — whether goods sit on an open shelf or behind glass, a priced display is ordinarily only an invitation to treat. The customer's insistence, or the item's identifiability, doesn't change that.

testPool.prompt: A company publishes a notice: 'We will pay £1,000 to the first person to find our missing dog, Max, and return him to this address by Friday, no further conditions.' Priya finds Max and returns him on Thursday, never having communicated with the company beforehand. Can she claim the £1,000?
options: Yes — following Carlill, this is a unilateral offer to the world, accepted by performing the stipulated act, and no advance communication of acceptance is required
No — because Priya never wrote to the company accepting the offer before looking for the dog
No — a company can never make a binding offer to an unascertained group of people
testPool.explanation: This mirrors Carlill precisely: a specific, unconditional promise made to whoever performs the stated act. Performance is the acceptance; nothing further needed to be communicated in advance.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact that marks the point at which the original offer was terminated.
testPool.scenarioText: A car dealer offers a used van for £6,000. The buyer says 'I'll give you £5,500.' The dealer says nothing for two days. The buyer then calls back and says 'actually, I accept your original £6,000 offer.'
testPool.explanation: The counter-offer of £5,500 is the moment the original £6,000 offer died. Everything that follows is the buyer trying to accept an offer that no longer legally exists.

testPool.prompt: Which letter is more likely to be treated as a genuine offer, applying the reasoning in Gibson v Manchester City Council?
testPool.scenarioA: 'The Council may be prepared to sell you this property at £9,500. This letter should not be regarded as a firm offer.'
testPool.scenarioB: 'I confirm the Council agrees to sell you this property at £9,500. Please sign and return the enclosed agreement so that we can proceed to completion.'
testPool.explanation: B uses committing, definite language pointing to a concrete next step (sign and return the agreement) — closer to Storer v Manchester CC, which was held to be an offer. A uses the exact disclaiming language from Gibson itself, held to be only an invitation to treat.

testPool.prompt: An auctioneer's catalogue lists a painting with a guide price of '£3,000–£4,000, no reserve.' A bidder claims the catalogue itself is a binding offer to sell at £3,000, the lower figure. Is this correct?
options: No — an auction catalogue and guide price are, like a shop display, generally only an invitation to treat; bids made at the auction are the offers, which the auctioneer's call accepts
Yes — a stated price range in a catalogue is always the binding offer price at its lowest figure
Yes, but only because the item was marked 'no reserve'
testPool.trapExplanation: The 'no reserve' detail is a distraction — it can affect the auctioneer's own obligations to conduct the sale fairly, but it does not turn the catalogue itself into a binding offer at the guide price. The catalogue invites bids; the bids are the offers.

testPool.prompt: A boutique places a mannequin in its shop window wearing a coat, with a small card reading 'This coat: £150 — enquire within.' A customer, Ade, walks in and says 'I'll take the coat in the window for £150', placing cash on the counter. The manager refuses to sell, saying the coat is the shop's last one and reserved for a photoshoot. Ade insists a contract was formed the moment he spoke. Analyse whether Ade is correct.
factsToOrder: The window display shows a specific coat with a stated price
Ade states he will take the coat at that price and offers payment
The manager refuses to sell, citing the coat's reserved status
Ade argues the display itself bound the shop to sell

scaffolds.support: Full model IRAC answer shown, with each fact mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule and Issue given; student drags facts into Application and writes Conclusion
Issue given only; student selects the Rule, drags facts into Application, writes Conclusion
No scaffold; student writes full IRAC unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether the window display, or alternatively Ade's statement at the counter, constituted a binding offer that the shop was obliged to accept.
modelAnswer.rule: A priced display of goods, whether on a shelf or in a window, is ordinarily only an invitation to treat (Boots; Fisher v Bell). The customer's own statement, offering to buy at the stated terms, is the offer; the seller remains free to accept or decline it (Boots).
modelAnswer.application: The mannequin display with the price card is an invitation to treat, not an offer — the shop never bound itself by putting the coat in the window. Ade's statement 'I'll take the coat for £150' with payment offered is his offer to buy. The manager is free to decline that offer, as Boots confirms happens at the till stage; the shop's reason (a reserved item) is irrelevant to whether it is legally entitled to refuse.
modelAnswer.conclusion: Ade is incorrect. No contract was formed by the display, and the manager was entitled to reject Ade's offer at the counter; no binding contract exists.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The most common mistake in this lesson's test items is treating any priced, specific-looking display or advert as automatically an offer. It almost never is — the display or advert is usually only step one, inviting someone else to make the actual offer, which the seller remains free to accept or refuse.
